newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss banks may have more Holocaust money - Volcker.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks may have more Holocaust money - Volcker.

text.p: Swiss banks may have more money from Holocaust victims in their vaults than a previous sweep of dormant accounts revealed, former U.S. central bank chief Paul Volcker said on Friday.

Volcker, who heads an independent committee hunting bank accounts left ownerless by Jews and other victims of Nazi persecution, said only 26 of 500 banks had responded to a government-mandated sweep of dormant accounts in 1962.
"This raises questions of how assidious everybody was in responding and how much follow-up there was," Volcker told a news conference following a meeting of his committee.
The lack of response by many banks in 1962 also raised the issue of how the questionaires were formulated and whether it was too easy for banks not to respond, Volcker said.
"I can assure you that our investigation will go beyond 26 banks," Volcker, who was chairman of the U.S. Federal Reserve from 1979 to 1987, said.
The first full-scale search for dormant accounts in Swiss banks in 1962 uncovered about 10 million Swiss francs.
Under pressure from Jewish organisations, banks in 1995 again searched their files for dormant accounts and this time they turned up another 40 million swiss francs ($28 million).
But Jewish organisations insist Swiss banks still have millions of dollars belonging to relatives of Holocaust victims.
The Swiss parliament has lifted the country's strict banking secrecy rules for the Volcker committee's auditors, but several months will go by before the banks' records are searched.
Separately, the Swiss Banking Commission said in a statement that the auditors of the Volcker commission would be granted free and unfettered access to all relevant banking files.
"This makes clear that our auditors have the full force of the Swiss regulatory authorities," Volcker commented.

Volcker said the schedule to audit banks had been set back a few months by Union Bank of Switzerland's (UBS) violation of a government ban on shredding documents that could be of use in the investigations.
Volcker, who was briefed by UBS's chief executive Mathis Cabiallavetta on Friday, termed the destruction of historic files an "unfortunate incident" that raised many questions.
Over the next two months the committee's auditing firms would examine the record destroying practices of Swiss banks.
"If this incident hadn't occurred, we wouldn't have to go through these steps," Volcker said.

Earlier this month a security guard working at UBS removed some documents from a batch that were due to be shredded and belonged to a UBS subsidiary active in Germany during the 1930s and 1940s. The other documents were shredded.

While Volcker said it was impossible to say whether relevant information had been lost from the shredding, he said UBS had explained the incident and told him that any customer records that would be relevant for the search were not affected.

Volcker said the committee, which comprises representatives of Jewish organisations and Swiss banks, was making progress. He was satisfied with the support he had received from all parties, including the Swiss government, banks and Jewish organisations.
He acknowledged the issue of money in Swiss banks from Holocaust victims was very emotional and had lead to "a lot of contoversy and accusations."
"But what is important is whether there is support for the process and I am satisfied there is," Volcker said.

He cautioned, however, against high expectations because 50 years had elapsed and accounts may have been closed for very legitimate reasons through bank mergers or bank closures. ($1=1.4193 Swiss Franc)
